lessons.title: How does a website work?
lessons.concept: Connect an address, a server and a page.

explanation.text: The browser is your shop window. The server prepares its contents.
A restaurant follows the same journey to display its menu.
Think of ordering at a counter: your browser requests /boutique, the server prepares the page, then you see it. An address is a request, not the contents.

lessons.title: Frontend and backend

explanation.text: The frontend takes the request. The backend decides whether it is valid.
A booking form must also check availability on the server.
A customer can write a price on paper. The cashier checks the real price before selling. Your API checks it on the server.

annotations.label: POST receives a creation request. req contains the browser request. NextRequest describes its type. The server must then validate the data before creating the order.

exercise.task: Which file receives order creation? Write its path.

quiz.explanation: No. The server must verify prices using its own data.

summary: No. The server must verify prices using its own data.
lessons.why: Checkout collects an order. POST in app/api/orders/route.ts receives the request and applies server rules.
lessons.whatIf: Without the POST export this route no longer handles creation with this function. It does not automatically become a Server Action.

lessons.title: Discover my project
lessons.concept: Recognize the tools that build your site.

explanation.text: package.json lists the tools and start commands.
Read this file first in another JavaScript project.
The project is a workshop. package.json lists its tools and commands: dev opens the workshop; build prepares the delivery.

annotations.label: dev names a shortcut. next dev starts the development server. Use this shortcut in the terminal by typing npm run dev.
build prepares the version to publish. This project uses a small Node.js script. This is different from running the development server.

exercise.task: Which command starts the local site?
hints: npm run, followed by the dev script name.
exercise.solution:
npm run dev
npm.cmd run dev

quiz.question: Which tool checks types?
quiz.explanation: No. npm run build also checks the production version.

summary: No. npm run build also checks the production version.
lessons.why: package.json lists Next.js 15, React 19 and project commands. package-lock.json locks installed versions. TypeScript helps catch invalid values.
lessons.whatIf:
Removing this entry removes the npm run dev shortcut. It does not uninstall Next.js.
npm run build loses its shortcut. Previously deployed files are not deleted by this change.

explanation.text: Each folder organizes one kind of work, like shelves in a store.

lessons.title: Understand layout.tsx
lessons.concept: Understand the shared frame around pages.

explanation.text: The layout is the frame. children is the page placed inside it.
A hotel site also keeps shared navigation around its pages.
The shop window and counter stay while displayed products change. The layout keeps the frame; children receives the current page.

codeExample.code:
children: React.ReactNode;
<main id="main-content" tabIndex={-1} className="flex-1 outline-none">{children}</main>

annotations.label: children is the content received by the frame. React.ReactNode says it can contain React UI. This type helps TypeScript detect invalid values.
main holds the page’s main content. {children} inserts the current page into the frame. id identifies this area; tabIndex allows programmatic focus.

exercise.task: Which word names the content received by RootLayout?
hints: Read the function parameters and their type.

quiz.question: Why share a layout?
quiz.explanation: Yes. The frame would have no route content.

summary: Yes. The frame would have no route content.
lessons.why: app/layout.tsx defines the HTML document and receives children, the current route content. Context providers share data such as the cart.
lessons.whatIf:
The TypeScript contract no longer declares children while the function uses it, so type checking reports a problem.
Removing this line also removes {children}: page content no longer appears in this main. The surrounding frame may still display.

lessons.title: My first component
lessons.concept: Recognize a reusable part of the interface.

explanation.text: A component is a mold. Different data produces different cards.
ProductCard can become HotelCard or ArticleCard with other data.
A product card is a mold: change the product, keep the shape. ProductCard avoids copying the same interface for every item.

annotations.label: ProductCard is the component name. It receives product. CardProduct describes the expected data. recommendation is optional and defaults to false. For now, remember: one card receives one product.
We read the product rating. ?? 0 uses zero if the rating is missing. Different input data can produce a different card.
product.name means “this product’s name”. Braces display its value. The component can therefore serve many products.

exercise.task: What would you call a reusable hotel card?
hints: Start a component name with a capital letter.

quiz.question: What problem does a component solve?
quiz.explanation: Yes. Every use of this component receives the change.

summary: Yes. Every use of this component receives the change.
lessons.why: ProductCard receives a product and returns its card. The same component can display many products without copying its structure.
lessons.whatIf:
Without product in the parameters, reads of product fail. recommendation = false is a default, not a required input.
Deleting the declaration leaves rating usages undefined. Removing only ?? 0 removes the fallback when a rating is missing.
The name disappears at this position. The product still exists: you removed its display, not its data.

lessons.title: Understand JSX

explanation.text: Tags form boxes. Braces put data inside them.
An article card uses the same tags for its title and image.
A label has a frame and text. h3 is the title frame; {product.name} puts the real name inside it.

annotations.label: h3 opens a heading. title supplies its tooltip. className chooses its style. line-clamp-2 limits text to two lines. styles.title comes from the card’s CSS file.
This is the visible text: the product name’s value. Without braces, you would show the words product.name instead of their value.
This tag closes the heading. / means “end of this element”. Everything between the two tags belongs to this heading.

exercise.task: In JSX, write how to display product.name.

quiz.question: Which property replaces class in JSX?
quiz.explanation: No. Between tags it would be literal text.

summary: No. Between tags it would be literal text.
lessons.why: JSX describes UI in a TypeScript file. A tag such as article contains elements; braces insert JavaScript values.
lessons.whatIf: Removing only the opening tag leaves an unmatched , invalid JSX. Removing just className changes styling. The name disappears at this position. The product still exists: you removed its display, not its data. The opening tag is no longer closed: JSX does not compile. The two tags form a pair.

The same classes can arrange hotel rooms or articles.
The same product can be arranged in a column or a row. CSS changes presentation without changing its name or price.

lessons.title: Understand useState
lessons.concept: Understand how React remembers a value on screen.

explanation.text: useState gives a value and a function to change it.
A form can remember a typed name with useState.
A whiteboard remembers the cart list. setItems rewrites it and tells React to update the screen. localStorage keeps a copy for the next visit.

codeExample.code:
const [items, setItems] = useState<CartItem[]>([]);
const [hydrated, setHydrated] = useState(false);

annotations.label: items is the current list. setItems changes it and asks React to update the screen. CartItem[] means a list of cart items. The final [] is the initial empty list.
Same pattern, different information: here a yes/no value. false means no. The value’s name changes, but the useState pattern stays the same.

exercise.task: Which function updates items in this file?
hints: The second name in brackets updates the first.

quiz.question: What does items represent?
quiz.explanation: No. Use React’s update mechanism, such as setItems.

summary: No. Use React’s update mechanism, such as setItems.
lessons.why: CartProvider uses items and setItems. items is the current list; setItems asks React to update the list and its display.
lessons.whatIf:
Without this declaration items and setItems are undefined. Replacing state with an ordinary variable does not itself trigger a React render.
Deleting hydrated breaks its usages. Removing the save guard can overwrite the stored cart with the initial empty list.

teaching.what: Understand how React remembers a value on screen.
teaching.why: CartProvider uses items and setItems. items is the current list; setItems asks React to update the list and its display.

teaching.breaks:
Without this declaration items and setItems are undefined. Replacing state with an ordinary variable does not itself trigger a React render.
Deleting hydrated breaks its usages. Removing the save guard can overwrite the stored cart with the initial empty list.
